title: Eppur non si trovano Vol. 3: Phoebe -- a Mirage of a Primordial Black Hole
comment: submitted to Acta Astronomica, comments on arXiv:2605.19332 and arXiv:2605.19375
summary: Recent preprints by Key et al. reported the discovery of a short-lived brightening of a star (nicknamed "Phoebe") located in the Large Magellanic Cloud that was interpreted as a short-timescale gravitational microlensing event produced by a lunar-mass primordial black hole (PBH) in the Milky Way dark matter halo. Here, we present an independent re-analysis of the publicly available DECam observations of this object, incorporating additional data from 2020 and 2021. The object underwent at least three distinct, low-amplitude brightenings (one of which was misinterpreted as a short-timescale microlensing event) in addition to long-term variations of its mean magnitude. These characteristics indicate that Phoebe is an ordinary variable star rather than a microlensing event. This finding resolves the apparent tension with the results from earlier microlensing experiments that rule out the hypothesis that a substantial fraction of dark matter is composed of lunar- and planetary-mass PBHs.

AI.tldr: Phoebe is an ordinary variable star, not a microlensing event from a primordial black hole, resolving the tension with previous dark matter constraints.
AI.motivation: To verify whether the short-lived brightening of star "Phoebe" was indeed a short-timescale gravitational microlensing event caused by a lunar-mass primordial black hole (PBH) in the Milky Way dark matter halo, as recently claimed.
AI.method: Independent re-analysis of publicly available DECam observations of Phoebe, incorporating additional data from 2020 and 2021.
AI.result: Phoebe exhibited at least three distinct, low-amplitude brightenings plus long-term mean magnitude variations, with one brightening misinterpreted as a short-timescale microlensing event.
AI.conclusion: Phoebe is an ordinary variable star, not a PBH microlensing event, resolving the apparent conflict with previous microlensing experiments that rule out a substantial dark matter fraction in lunar- and planetary-mass PBHs.

title: Reimagining SED Fitting with Cosmological Galaxy Simulations and Machine Learning
comment: 33 pages, 22 figures. To be submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics. Comments welcome. A basic installation procedure for PHOT-GAL is available at https://github.com/DhruvZ/Phot-Gal
summary: SED fitting is the most common technique to recover galaxy physical properties from observed photometry. However, SED fitting requires many assumptions that essentially collapse a galaxy from a three-dimensional spatially varying object with complex structure into a scalar point. Moreover, modern inference techniques are computationally intensive, which presents a unique challenge in the era of extremely large datasets. We present \textsc{Phot-Gal}, a new galaxy SED modeling tool that solves the inverse problem of SED fitting by training a machine learning model on photometry generated from 3D radiative transfer of simulated galaxies with a wide range of implemented physics. \textsc{Phot-Gal} is designed to accept an arbitrary amount of input photometry by utilizing a $K$-nearest neighbors imputation strategy. Our fiducial model predicts redshift, stellar mass, dust mass, and star formation rate with uncertainties based on the provided input photometry. We evaluate the performance of \textsc{Phot-Gal} relative to the commonly-used SED fitting tool \textsc{prospector} in successfully recovering each of these properties with several metrics for the inferred values and uncertainties and find that it outperforms the accuracy of standard SED fitting software on the testing set. However, with fewer photometric constraints, \textsc{Phot-Gal} is more likely to have output uncertainties that do not reflect the offset from the ground truth. We dissect the components of \textsc{Phot-Gal} to find reasonable physical justifications for the photometry it relies on most, understand how each step in its workflow contributes to the eventual output posterior, and evaluate its ability to generalize to novel data.

AI.tldr: Phot-Gal is a machine learning-based SED fitting tool that uses 3D radiative transfer simulations and K-nearest neighbors imputation to predict galaxy properties (redshift, stellar mass, dust mass, SFR) from photometry, outperforming traditional tools like Prospector in accuracy but showing limitations in uncertainty quantification with sparse inputs.
AI.motivation: Traditional SED fitting collapses 3D galaxy structure into scalar points, relies on computationally intensive inference, and faces scalability challenges with large datasets. Phot-Gal aims to solve the inverse problem more efficiently using machine learning trained on 3D radiative transfer simulations.
AI.method: Phot-Gal trains a machine learning model on photometry generated from 3D radiative transfer simulations of galaxies with diverse physics. It uses K-nearest neighbors imputation to handle arbitrary numbers of input photometric bands. The model predicts redshift, stellar mass, dust mass, and SFR with associated uncertainties.
AI.result: Phot-Gal outperforms Prospector in accuracy on the testing set across multiple metrics. However, with fewer photometric constraints, its output uncertainties are less reliable (not reflecting offset from ground truth). The paper dissects model components, identifies physically justifiable photometric dependencies, and evaluates generalization to novel data.
AI.conclusion: Phot-Gal offers a faster, more accurate alternative to traditional SED fitting for large datasets, though caution is needed with sparse photometry where uncertainty calibration degrades. The model's reliance on specific photometric bands is physically interpretable.

title: Baryonic mass budgets in the central regions of the Bullet Cluster and their consistency with strong lensing in MOND
summary: Strong lensing observations of the Bullet Cluster have traditionally been regarded as strong evidence for dark matter and a major challenge to Milgromian dynamics (MOND). The offset between the lensing mass and the X-ray gas centroids implies a substantial amount of unseen mass near the brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs). However, the high metallicities observed in both the intracluster gas and the massive early-type member galaxies suggest a past stellar population dominated by massive stars, whose evolved remnants contribute additional baryonic mass. This effect is naturally incorporated in the integrated galaxy-wide initial mass function (IGIMF) theory, which predicts substantially larger baryonic masses than a canonical IMF. In this work, we re-estimate the baryonic masses of the three BCG-centred core regions of the Bullet Cluster and compare them with MOND strong-lensing masses. We derive IGIMF masses using stellar population synthesis models with constant and (self-) enriched metallicities, representing lower and upper mass limits, respectively. We find that the MOND strong-lensing masses of all three cores lie within the range predicted by the IGIMF models. These results suggest that the baryonic mass budget inferred under the IGIMF framework is consistent with MOND requirements in the core regions of the Bullet Cluster. However, the physical viability of this scenario also depends on the spatial distribution and dynamical behavior of the remnant population, which remain to be established. More generally, regardless of the validity of MOND, the results imply that less dark matter may be required than previously inferred.

AI.tldr: The paper re-analyzes the Bullet Cluster's strong lensing data under MOND using the IGIMF framework, finding that MOND-predicted masses in the three core regions are consistent with the baryonic masses derived from IGIMF models, suggesting less dark matter may be needed than previously thought.
AI.motivation: The Bullet Cluster's lensing mass-X-ray offset has been considered strong evidence for dark matter and a challenge to MOND. This work revisits that challenge by considering that the integrated galaxy-wide initial mass function (IGIMF) predicts larger baryonic masses from evolved stellar remnants than the canonical IMF, potentially reconciling MOND with observations.
AI.method: The study re-estimates baryonic masses of three BCG-centred core regions of the Bullet Cluster using stellar population synthesis models under the IGIMF theory, with constant and (self-)enriched metallicities as lower and upper mass limits. These are then compared with MOND strong-lensing masses.
AI.result: MOND strong-lensing masses for all three cores lie within the mass range predicted by IGIMF models, indicating consistency between the baryonic mass budget (under IGIMF) and MOND requirements in the cluster cores.
AI.conclusion: The IGIMF framework can potentially resolve the tension between MOND and Bullet Cluster strong lensing observations, though the spatial distribution and dynamics of remnant populations need further validation. Regardless of MOND's validity, the results imply that less dark matter may be required than previously inferred.

title: Characterizing the Formation and Evolution of S0-galaxies (CaFES-0): Their formation pathways around Galaxy Clusters
comment: Submitted to Astronomy and Astrophysics. 12 pages, 10 figures, 1 appendix
summary: The formation pathways of lenticular galaxies (S0s), which lie morphologically between elliptical and spiral galaxies, remain a topic of active research. Environmental effects, merging histories, and pre-processing mechanisms are often proposed as key factors influencing their transformation. However, the relative importance of these processes remains unclear, particularly when compared with other galaxy types. We use the Hydrangea cosmological zoom-in simulation suite to analyse the environmental histories of S0 galaxies, defined here as central and satellite quenched disk galaxies. We find that the vast majority (>85\%) of our sample of S0s are satellites in massive haloes (log$_{10}$M$_{200}/$M$_\odot$ > 13), while only $\sim10\%$ are centrals in low-mass haloes. Satellite S0s exhibit a highly quiescent merging history, with $\sim60\%$ experiencing no significant mergers since $z=2$. Centrals show more varied merging histories, although our results may be affected by limited sample size. Contrary to expectations, no clear trends in merger ratios with morphology are observed. However, mergers involving lenticular and spiral galaxies tend to occur in low-density environments and are likely gas-rich, enabling disk reformation. Pre-processing effects in groups are critical, influencing both quenching and morphological transformation.} Our results strongly suggest that S0 galaxies predominantly form from faded/stripped spirals in clusters, with a minority forming via mergers in smaller haloes. These results are in agreement with previous observations of lenticular galaxies around galaxy clusters.

AI.tldr: Using Hydrangea simulations, the study finds that >85% of lenticular galaxies (S0s) are satellites in massive halos with quiescent merger histories, forming primarily from faded/stripped spirals in clusters, while only ~10% are centrals in low-mass halos formed via mergers.
AI.motivation: The formation pathways of lenticular galaxies (S0s) remain poorly understood, particularly regarding the relative importance of environmental effects, merging histories, and pre-processing mechanisms compared to other galaxy types.
AI.method: Analysis of S0 galaxies (defined as central and satellite quenched disk galaxies) using the Hydrangea cosmological zoom-in simulation suite to study their environmental and merging histories.
AI.result: >85% of S0s are satellites in massive halos (log₁₀M₂₀₀/M☉>13), ~60% experienced no significant mergers since z=2. Only ~10% are centrals in low-mass halos. No clear trends in merger ratios with morphology; mergers involving lenticular/spiral galaxies occur in low-density gas-rich environments enabling disk reformation. Pre-processing in groups critically influences quenching and morphological transformation.
AI.conclusion: S0 galaxies predominantly form from faded/stripped spirals in clusters, with a minority forming via mergers in smaller haloes, consistent with previous cluster observations.

title: Steady-state Stellar Winds Driven by Recombination
summary: Hydrogen and helium recombination energy has been proposed as a potential driver of mass ejection in common-envelope evolution and other eruptive stellar phenomena. We investigate whether recombination can by itself launch a steady, transonic wind from near a stellar surface. Using a tabulated equation of state, we explore steady-state, adiabatic wind solutions over a broad range of stellar mass, density, and temperature. We classify a wind as recombination-driven only if the gas is gravitationally bound prior to recombination and if the released energy remains trapped until the flow becomes unbound. Only a small fraction of the solutions satisfy both conditions. In most cases, the gas is either already unbound without recombination or loses the released energy through radiative diffusion while still bound. The subset of valid solutions require outflow velocities $\gtrsim 10\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ at $10\,R_\odot$, inconsistent with a wind launched from a hydrostatic star. We conclude that recombination energy alone is unlikely to produce steady stellar winds. It can, however, accelerate and unbind a pre-existing outflow generated by processes such as binary orbital decay, producing mass-loss rates of $\sim \rm M_\odot\,yr^{-1}$.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether hydrogen and helium recombination energy alone can drive steady, transonic winds from stellar surfaces. Using a tabulated equation of state and adiabatic wind models, the authors find that only a small fraction of solutions satisfy conditions for recombination-driven winds. They conclude that recombination energy alone is unlikely to produce steady stellar winds but can accelerate pre-existing outflows from binary interactions.
AI.motivation: To test the hypothesis that recombination energy from hydrogen and helium can launch steady, transonic winds from stellar surfaces, as previously proposed for driving mass ejection in common-envelope evolution and other eruptive stellar phenomena.
AI.method: Steady-state, adiabatic wind solutions were explored using a tabulated equation of state across a broad parameter space of stellar mass, density, and temperature. Winds were classified as recombination-driven only if the gas was gravitationally bound before recombination and the released energy remained trapped until the flow became unbound.
AI.result: Only a small fraction of solutions satisfied both conditions for recombination-driven winds. In most cases, the gas was already unbound without recombination or lost the released energy through radiative diffusion while still bound. Valid solutions required outflow velocities ≥10 km/s at 10 R⊙, inconsistent with a wind launched from a hydrostatic star.
AI.conclusion: Recombination energy alone is unlikely to produce steady stellar winds, but it can accelerate and unbind pre-existing outflows from processes like binary orbital decay, potentially producing mass-loss rates of ~M⊙/yr.

title: On the later evolution of observationally selected protocluster candidates at $z\,{\gtrsim}\,5$
summary: Recent observations have revealed numerous protocluster candidates at $z\,{\gtrsim}\,5$, yet whether these systems will eventually evolve into today's galaxy clusters remains an open question. Using the FLAMINGO simulations -- resolving protocluster cores up to $z\,{\simeq}\,10$ -- we track the later evolution of observationally selected protocluster candidates, comparing three selection methods against observational samples. The observed number density falls between our mass-selected and abundance-matched samples, implying that current searches pick up both genuine cluster progenitors and significant interlopers that will not reach cluster masses by $z\,{=}\,0$. We find that candidates at $z\gtrsim5$ are heavily clustered, hosting 2$-$10 neighbors within 10\,cMpc. Consequently, a candidate with a neighbor at 5\,cMpc (10\,cMpc) faces a $\gtrsim50\%$ ($\gtrsim30\%$) probability of later merging into a larger system, mostly at $z\,{\lesssim}\,2$. The merger count converges beyond ${\sim}10$\,cMpc, pointing to a fundamental scale in structure formation. Observations show markedly weaker clustering than our simulations predict, suggesting clustering offers a currently overlooked diagnostic. Each candidate undergoes roughly 2$-$6 later major mergers, mostly with systems too small to be recognized as massive at the selection epoch. Hence, relying solely on high-$z$ mass and galaxy overdensity to forecast a candidate's fate is prone to severe scatter and systematic error. A robust identification of true cluster progenitors demands a total mass sum of galaxies down to the faintest levels within a 10\,cMpc radius. Upcoming surveys with both depth and area will be key to reliably linking high-$z$ protocluster candidates to their ultimate destiny.

AI.tldr: Using FLAMINGO simulations, this study evaluates observational selection methods for z≳5 protocluster candidates, finding that current searches include both genuine progenitors and interlopers. Candidates are heavily clustered (2-10 neighbors within 10 cMpc) with significant merger probabilities, and observed clustering is weaker than simulations predict. Reliable identification requires summing galaxy masses within 10 cMpc down to faintest levels.
AI.motivation: Numerous protocluster candidates at z≳5 have been observed, but it remains unclear whether these systems will evolve into today's galaxy clusters.
AI.method: Used FLAMINGO simulations (resolving protocluster cores up to z≃10) to track later evolution of observationally selected protocluster candidates, comparing three selection methods against observational samples. Analyzed clustering properties, merger counts, and identification reliability.
AI.result: Observed number density falls between mass-selected and abundance-matched samples. Candidates at z≳5 host 2-10 neighbors within 10 cMpc; clustering is weaker in observations than simulations. Each candidate undergoes roughly 2-6 later major mergers, mostly with systems too small to be recognized as massive at selection epoch.
AI.conclusion: Robust identification of true cluster progenitors requires total mass sum of galaxies down to faintest levels within 10 cMpc radius. Reliable linking of high-z protocluster candidates to their ultimate destiny demands upcoming surveys with both depth and area.

title: An Ultramassive White Dwarf with a Likely Oxygen-Neon Core
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The core composition of ultramassive white dwarfs remains an open question in stellar evolution. The carbon content of white dwarf cores is critical to their role as progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. However, because the stellar photosphere only extends to the outermost layer of the star, observational probes of core compositions are limited. Here we present gravitational redshift measurements of an ultramassive white dwarf, SDSS J060851.44-005950.3, which indicate the likely presence of an oxygen-neon core. We measure the mass ($1.226_{-0.025}^{+0.024} M_\odot$) and radius ($0.491_{-0.009}^{+0.009}~R_\oplus$) of the white dwarf using gravitational redshifts from high-resolution UVES and MagE spectra paired with independent constraints from photometry. By comparing to state-of-the-art mass-radius relations for ultramassive white dwarfs, we find preference for a oxygen-neon core over a carbon-oxygen core, with a Bayes factor of $2.7$. This is a white dwarf which is likely structurally incapable of producing a Type Ia supernova, according to current understanding of supernova physics. This object provides evidence that white dwarfs which pass through the Q-branch without experiencing a delay in cooling compared to the normal white dwarf cooling sequence likely have oxygen-neon cores.

AI.tldr: Gravitational redshift measurements of the ultramassive white dwarf SDSS J060851.44-005950.3 reveal a mass of 1.226 M☉ and radius of 0.491 R⊕, with a Bayes factor of 2.7 favoring an oxygen-neon core over a carbon-oxygen core. This white dwarf is unlikely to produce a Type Ia supernova, providing evidence that white dwarfs passing through the Q-branch without cooling delay likely have ONe cores.
AI.motivation: The core composition of ultramassive white dwarfs remains an open question, and the carbon content of their cores is critical for understanding their role as Type Ia supernova progenitors. However, observational probes are limited because the photosphere only extends to the outermost layer, so direct measurements of core compositions are scarce.
AI.method: The authors used gravitational redshift measurements from high-resolution UVES and MagE spectra, paired with independent photometric constraints, to measure the mass and radius of the white dwarf. They then compared these measurements to state-of-the-art mass-radius relations for ultramassive white dwarfs and used Bayesian analysis to determine the most likely core composition.
AI.result: The white dwarf has a mass of 1.226−0.025+0.024 M☉ and radius of 0.491−0.009+0.009 R⊕. A Bayes factor of 2.7 favors an oxygen-neon core over a carbon-oxygen core. The object is structurally incapable of producing a Type Ia supernova under current understanding.
AI.conclusion: This work presents evidence that ultramassive white dwarfs passing through the Q-branch without experiencing a cooling delay likely have oxygen-neon cores, and provides direct observational constraints on the core composition of these objects.

title: Something green beneath the surface: The dynamical nature of Fossil Structures in IllustrisTNG-100
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Fossil structures (FS) have traditionally been considered dynamically relaxed end-products of group evolution, characterized by a large magnitude gap ($Δm_{1,2} \geq 2$). However, recent observations and simulations suggest this picture is incomplete. We investigate whether FS are dynamically relaxed systems and how their galaxy populations differ from non-fossil systems (non-FS), focusing on system dynamics and evolution of the galaxies inside them. Using \textsc{IllustrisTNG-100}, we select 182 structures ($M_{200} > 10^{13}\,M_{\odot}$) at $z = 0$, classifying them as FS/non-FS based on $Δm_{1,2}$ in the $r$-band. We track $Δm_{1,2}$ evolution over 9\,Gyr and analyze: (1) the emergence of $Δm_{1,2}$, (2) the fraction of quenched galaxies (sSFR $< 10^{-11}$\,yr$^{-1}$), (3) the distribution of galaxies in color--stellar mass space, and (4) the gas--BSG centroid shift as a dynamical proxy. The magnitude gap in FS is primarily driven by the absence of massive recent accretion: FS exhibit significantly lower BSG-to-satellite stellar mass ratios ($μ^{\rm{FS}}{\star}$=0.17 vs. $μ^{\rm{NFS}}{\star}$=0.39) for the most massive satellite accreted within the last 6\,Gyr. FS also host a more prominent red sequence and marginally higher quenched fractions than non-FS. Our findings indicate that while the magnitude gap effectively identifies systems that have ceased major mergers in the last 3-6 Gyr, it is a poor proxy for their current global dynamical state. Both FS and non-FS populations exhibit intermediate gas-BSG offsets ($D_{BSG-CM} \approx 0.15 R/R_{200}$), failing to reach full relaxation. This decoupling suggests that the magnitude gap traces the assembly history of massive components rather than the overall stability of the intra cluster medium.

AI.tldr: Using IllustrisTNG-100 simulations, the authors study 182 galaxy structures and find that fossil systems (FS) are characterized by a lack of recent massive accretion and a more prominent red sequence, but the magnitude gap is a poor proxy for dynamical relaxation, as both FS and non-FS show intermediate gas-BCG centroid offsets (~0.15 R/R200).
AI.motivation: To challenge the traditional view that fossil structures (FS) are dynamically relaxed end-products of group evolution, and to investigate whether FS are truly relaxed systems and how their galaxy populations differ from non-fossil systems.
AI.method: Using IllustrisTNG-100 simulation data, the authors selected 182 structures with M200 > 10^13 M⊙ at z=0, classifying them as FS/non-FS based on the r-band magnitude gap Δm1,2. They tracked Δm1,2 evolution over 9 Gyr and analyzed: (1) emergence of the magnitude gap, (2) quenched fraction (sSFR < 10^-11 yr^-1), (3) color-stellar mass distribution, and (4) gas-BCG centroid shift as a dynamical proxy.
AI.result: The magnitude gap in FS is primarily driven by the absence of massive recent accretion (μ⋆FS=0.17 vs. μ⋆NFS=0.39). FS host a more prominent red sequence and marginally higher quenched fractions. However, both FS and non-FS exhibit intermediate gas-BCG offsets (DBSG-CM ≈ 0.15 R/R200), indicating neither population is fully relaxed.
AI.conclusion: While the magnitude gap effectively identifies systems that have ceased major mergers in the last 3-6 Gyr, it is a poor proxy for current global dynamical state. The decoupling between magnitude gap and dynamical relaxation suggests that Δm1,2 traces assembly history of massive components, not overall ICM stability.

title: X-Shooter survey of disk accretion in Upper Scorpius II. A lack of correlation between accretion rates and disk properties
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: The evolution of protoplanetary discs is intertwined with the process of planet formation, growth and migration. Studies of nearby star forming regions of different ages and properties provide the necessary information needed to understand the processes dictating their evolution. This paper presents the results of a spectroscopic study of the stellar and accretion properties of a large sample of 127 stars with protoplanetary discs in the Upper Scorpius region with disc dust masses inferred from ALMA continuum measurements. The accretion luminosity is derived from the excess UV continuum emission with respect to the photospheric and chromospheric one self-consistently with the stellar spectral types, extinction and luminosity, using FRAPPE. We apply a new method to evaluate upper limits to the accretion luminosity. In ~50% of cases we evaluate upper limits on the accretion luminosity, either because the S/N of the data is insufficient or because the measured value of the accretion luminosity is below the estimate of the emission due to chromospheric activity. The results show that the mass accretion rate has a weak correlation with the stellar mass, while no correlation is observed with disc properties such as dust mass or gas disc radius. The dispersion is larger than what is found in younger star forming regions such as Lupus and Cham. I, and suggests a fading of the correlations with age. We find no evidence that membership to Upper Scorpius sub-groups, nor the properties of known binary or transition discs can explain the origin of this dispersion. The lack of correlation and large dispersion of accretion rates challenge the current expectations of evolutionary models. The observed properties point to a decoupling of the inner and outer disc by the age of Upper Scorpius and a fading of the relations observed in younger star forming regions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a spectroscopic study of 127 stars with protoplanetary discs in Upper Scorpius, finding that mass accretion rates show weak correlation with stellar mass and no correlation with disc properties (dust mass or gas disc radius). The large dispersion in accretion rates suggests a decoupling of inner and outer discs by the age of Upper Scorpius (~5-10 Myr), challenging current evolutionary models.
AI.motivation: To understand how protoplanetary disc evolution, planet formation, and accretion processes change with age by studying an older star-forming region (Upper Scorpius, ~5-10 Myr) and comparing with younger regions like Lupus and Chamaeleon I.
AI.method: Spectroscopic study of 127 stars with protoplanetary discs in Upper Scorpius using FRAPPE to derive accretion luminosity from UV excess continuum emission, self-consistently accounting for photospheric and chromospheric contributions, stellar spectral types, extinction, and luminosity. A new method for evaluating upper limits on accretion luminosity was applied.
AI.result: ~50% of cases yielded only upper limits on accretion luminosity. Mass accretion rate shows weak correlation with stellar mass and no correlation with disc dust mass or gas disc radius. The dispersion in accretion rates is larger than in younger regions (Lupus, Cham. I), indicating fading correlations with age. No evidence that sub-group membership, binarity, or transition disc properties explain the dispersion.
AI.conclusion: The lack of correlation and large dispersion challenge current evolutionary models. The observed properties suggest a decoupling of inner and outer discs by the age of Upper Scorpius, with a fading of the relations observed in younger star-forming regions.

title: PMO Polaris CO survey. II. Where is the dust?
summary: Dust plays critical chemical and dynamical roles in the interstellar medium (ISM), but its specific association with molecular and atomic gas remains difficult to isolate. Combining the PMO Polaris CO Survey (PPCOS), EBHIS \ion{H}{I} data, and \textit{Planck} dust maps, this study investigates dust distributions across multiple gas components in the Polaris Flare. We employ multi-technique linear decomposition -- including full-spectrum fitting and a regularization approach -- to reconstruct the dust distribution from multi-component gas emissions. This framework quantifies dust contributions from CO-associated, \ion{H}{I}-associated, and CO-dark molecular gas phases. CO-associated dust accounts for 20--40\% of the total dust mass, whereas dust in the broad \ion{H}{I} (warm neutral medium, WNM) component is negligible. Instead, \ion{H}{I}-associated dust concentrates primarily within the narrow cold neutral medium (CNM) and a distinct, ultra-narrow component with a velocity width comparable to the \ion{H}{I} spectral resolution. Residual dust at atomic-to-molecular (\ion{H}{I}--CO) interfaces contributes 4--10\% to the global dust mass, but exceeds 25\% at molecular cloud boundaries, confirming a substantial presence of CO-dark molecular gas. Furthermore, the velocity fields of dust-associated \ion{H}{I} closely match those of CO, indicating active dynamical coupling between CO-emitting gas and the surrounding CNM. Guided by these results, we present a stepwise schematic cartoon illustrating the coupling between multi-phase gas structures, molecular formation, and dust growth.

AI.tldr: This study uses multi-technique linear decomposition of CO, HI, and Planck dust data to quantify dust distributions across different gas phases in the Polaris Flare. CO-associated dust accounts for 20–40% of total dust mass, HI-associated dust is mainly in the cold neutral medium (CNM), and residual dust at atomic-to-molecular interfaces contributes 4–10% globally but >25% at cloud boundaries, confirming CO-dark molecular gas. Velocity fields show dynamical coupling between CO gas and surrounding CNM.
AI.motivation: Dust plays critical chemical and dynamical roles in the ISM, but its specific association with molecular and atomic gas is difficult to isolate.
AI.method: Combined PMO Polaris CO Survey (PPCOS), EBHIS HI data, and Planck dust maps; employed multi-technique linear decomposition including full-spectrum fitting and a regularization approach to reconstruct dust distribution from multi-component gas emissions.
AI.result: CO-associated dust: 20–40% of total dust mass; broad HI (WNM) dust negligible; HI-associated dust concentrated in CNM and an ultra-narrow component; residual dust at HI–CO interfaces contributes 4–10% globally but >25% at molecular cloud boundaries; velocity fields of dust-associated HI match those of CO.
AI.conclusion: Confirmed substantial CO-dark molecular gas at cloud boundaries; demonstrated active dynamical coupling between CO-emitting gas and surrounding CNM; presented a stepwise schematic cartoon illustrating multi-phase gas coupling, molecular formation, and dust growth.

title: Simulation to a Newborn Supernova Remnant from a Low-mass Iron Core Star
summary: Supernova remnant observations show a high degree of asymmetry, mixing, and inhomogeneity. These asymmetries are seeded during the early seconds of the explosion and are further enhanced and modified as the shock and ejecta move through the stellar progenitor and into the circumstellar medium. We present simulations of a 9.6 solar mass zero-metallicity progenitor initialized after shock revival and evolved for several years when the ejecta is in the circumstellar medium. A suite of 1D and 2D simulations examines the effects of neutron-star wind and radioactive decay heating. In 1D, decay heating forms a low-density bubble that suppresses the reverse shock. While in 2D, the heating is localized to metal-rich pockets, inflating them and compressing the surrounding material into dense shells. In 3D the neutron-star wind and decay heating modify the plume morphology, producing more large-scale structures. The extended plume morphology leads to an asymmetrical shock breakout. After breakout, the leading plumes cannot keep up with the shock front, resulting in deceleration and fragmentation by the reverse shock while retaining the large-scale asymmetry. The projected ejecta morphology and velocities are strongly viewing angle dependent. The relatively uniform metal-rich distribution does not resemble the strongly inhomogeneous ejecta structure of Cas A. The 160-isotope decay network shows that 24.4% of the radioactive heating comes from decay chains other than the canonical Ni-56 chain. The low explosion energy, low Ni-56 yield, and Ni/Fe ratio greater than unity suggest an observational signature similar to an electron capture supernova.

AI.tldr: Simulations of a 9.6 solar mass zero-metallicity progenitor show that neutron-star wind and radioactive decay heating significantly influence supernova remnant asymmetry, plume morphology, and shock breakout, with viewing-angle-dependent ejecta morphology and 24.4% of radioactive heating from non-canonical decay chains, resembling an electron capture supernova.
AI.motivation: To understand how neutron-star wind and radioactive decay heating seed and modify asymmetries, mixing, and inhomogeneities in supernova remnants from the early explosion phase through several years of evolution into the circumstellar medium.
AI.method: Suite of 1D, 2D, and 3D simulations of a 9.6 solar mass zero-metallicity progenitor initialized after shock revival and evolved for several years, incorporating a 160-isotope decay network to track radioactive heating contributions.
AI.result: Decay heating creates low-density bubbles suppressing the reverse shock in 1D; in 2D, it inflates metal-rich pockets and compresses surrounding material into dense shells; in 3D, it modifies plume morphology toward larger-scale structures. Asymmetrical shock breakout occurs, with leading plumes decelerating and fragmenting but retaining large-scale asymmetry. Ejecta morphology is strongly viewing-angle dependent. 24.4% of radioactive heating comes from non-Ni-56 decay chains. The metal-rich distribution is relatively uniform, unlike Cas A's inhomogeneous structure.
AI.conclusion: The low explosion energy, low Ni-56 yield, and Ni/Fe ratio > 1 suggest observational signatures similar to an electron capture supernova, and the ejecta structure does not match the highly inhomogeneous morphology of Cas A.

title: Evolution of starless cores in massive clumps seen by the ALMA ASHES and QUARKS surveys
summary: We present a systematic comparative analysis of 324 starless cores in early-phase infrared-dark clouds (IRDCs; ASHES survey) and evolved-phase infrared-bright clouds (IRBCs; QUARKS survey) using 1.3 mm continuum and line data by the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA). Despite having comparable sizes ($\sim$2500 au),starless cores in IRBCs exhibit systematically higher median mass ($1.5\,M_{\odot}$ vs. $0.6\,M_{\odot}$), number density, and surface density--enhancements of approximately a factor of two relative to starless cores in IRDCs. Starless cores in IRBCs also display relatively stronger non-thermal motions ($\rmσ\sim 0.5\,km\,s^{-1}$ vs. $\rm0.3\,km\,s^{-1}$), higher total virial parameters (median $α_{\mathrm{vir,tot}} \sim$ 2.3 vs. 1.0), and steeper density profiles, indicating more centrally concentrated structures in feedback-driven, turbulence-enhanced environments. These findings support a dual evolutionary origin: (i) new core formation in evolved IRBCs under altered initial conditions, and (ii) subsequent dynamical mass growth via accretion from extended reservoirs. The prevalence of low-mass starless cores--even in late-stage IRBC environments--challenges models requiring massive prestellar cores and instead favors competitive-like dynamical mass accretion scenarios for high-mass star formation.

AI.tldr: A comparative ALMA 1.3 mm survey of 324 starless cores in early-phase IRDCs (ASHES) and evolved-phase IRBCs (QUARKS) finds that IRBC cores are systematically more massive (~1.5 M☉ vs. 0.6 M☉), denser, more turbulent, and more centrally concentrated, supporting dual evolutionary origins (new core formation under altered conditions plus accretion-driven mass growth) and favoring competitive accretion over massive prestellar cores for high-mass star formation.
AI.motivation: To systematically compare the physical properties (mass, density, kinematics, structure) of starless cores between early-phase infrared-dark clouds (IRDCs) and evolved-phase infrared-bright clouds (IRBCs), to understand how core properties evolve and what mechanisms drive high-mass star formation.
AI.method: Systematic comparative analysis of 324 starless cores using 1.3 mm continuum and line data from ALMA:  cores in early-phase IRDCs from the ASHES survey vs. cores in evolved-phase IRBCs from the QUARKS survey.
AI.result: Starless cores in IRBCs have systematically higher median mass (1.5 M☉ vs. 0.6 M☉), number density, and surface density (~2× enhancement), stronger non-thermal motions (σ~0.5 vs. 0.3 km/s), higher virial parameters (α_vir,tot~2.3 vs. 1.0), and steeper density profiles, indicating more centrally concentrated structures in feedback-driven, turbulent environments.
AI.conclusion: Supports a dual evolutionary origin: (i) new core formation in evolved IRBCs under altered initial conditions, and (ii) subsequent dynamical mass growth via accretion from extended reservoirs. The prevalence of low-mass starless cores even in late-stage IRBCs challenges massive prestellar core models and favors competitive-like dynamical mass accretion scenarios for high-mass star formation.

title: Review of Machine Learning Models for Solar Energetic Particle Prediction
comment: Review Paper, Maine text: 23 pages, References: 5 pages, Appendix: 42 pages
summary: Solar energetic particle (SEP) events have attracted increasing attention due to their significant radiation hazards for aviation, spacecraft electronics, and human missions beyond Earth's magnetosphere. From a scientific perspective, SEP events are intriguing because they arise from a set of physical processes extending from the solar surface and corona through the heliosphere, offering insight into particle acceleration and transport mechanisms that are widely applicable across astrophysics. Therefore, advancing our ability to understand and predict SEP events is essential both for deepening our knowledge of such mechanisms and for safeguarding space technologies and exploration. Traditionally, researchers have modeled SEPs using physics-based simulations and empirical methods. More recently, machine learning (ML) has emerged as a new tool for understanding and predicting SEP events. The purpose of this manuscript is to review the currently available ML models for SEP prediction, identify the datasets used for training, compare their architectures, inputs, and outputs, and, based on these insights, outline good practices and recommendations for future research.

AI.tldr: This review systematically examines machine learning models for solar energetic particle (SEP) event prediction, covering datasets, architectures, inputs/outputs, and offering recommendations for future research.
AI.motivation: SEP events pose radiation hazards to aviation, spacecraft, and human space missions, and understanding their underlying particle acceleration and transport mechanisms is important for astrophysics. Improving SEP prediction is essential for both scientific knowledge and safeguarding space technologies.
AI.method: The paper reviews available ML models for SEP prediction, identifies training datasets, compares model architectures, inputs, and outputs, and synthesizes good practices and recommendations.
AI.result: A comprehensive comparison of ML-based SEP prediction models, including their datasets, architectural choices, input features, and output formats.
AI.conclusion: The review outlines good practices and actionable recommendations to guide future research in ML-driven SEP prediction.

title: Multi-band Structural Analysis of KiDS-selected Low Surface Brightness Galaxies with Hyper Suprime-Cam Imaging
summary: We present a homogeneous multi-band structural analysis of 205 KiDS-selected low surface brightness galaxy (LSBG) candidates using deep Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) $G$, $R$, and $I$-band imaging. Structural parameters were derived using single-component Sérsic modeling with GALFIT. The sample is dominated by diffuse systems with low Sérsic indices, with the distributions consistently peaking near $n\approx0.7$ across all bands. The estimated $B$-band central surface brightness distribution has a median value of $\tildeμ_{0,B}=24.55$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$, indicating that the galaxies lie firmly within the low surface brightness regime. The catalog is strongly dominated by red systems, comprising 178 red LSBGs (87.3$\%$) and 27 blue LSBGs (12.7$\%$). Despite this color bimodality, the red and blue subsamples show similar structural properties, with no statistically significant differences in Sérsic index, effective radius, axis ratio, or surface brightness distributions. The absence of a correlation between color and axis ratio further suggests that dust reddening is unlikely to be the primary driver of the red colors. Overall, the sample provides a well-characterized structural reference set of LSBGs in the HSC footprint and confirms that the KiDS selected candidates are predominantly genuine low surface brightness galaxies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a structural analysis of 205 low surface brightness galaxy (LSBG) candidates using multi-band HSC imaging, finding they are predominantly diffuse (Sérsic index ~0.7), red (87.3%), and structurally similar regardless of color, confirming the KiDS selection reliably identifies genuine LSBGs.
AI.motivation: To characterize the structural properties of KiDS-selected LSBG candidates using deeper, higher-resolution multi-band HSC imaging to verify their nature as genuine low surface brightness galaxies and understand their physical properties.
AI.method: Multi-band (G, R, I) structural analysis of 205 LSBG candidates using single-component Sérsic modeling with GALFIT on deep Hyper Suprime-Cam imaging, with color classification into red and blue subsamples and statistical comparisons of structural parameters.
AI.result: The sample is dominated by diffuse systems with Sérsic indices peaking near n≈0.7 across all bands. The median B-band central surface brightness is 24.55 mag arcsec⁻². The catalog is 87.3% red and 12.7% blue. Red and blue subsamples show no statistically significant differences in structural properties. No correlation between color and axis ratio indicates dust reddening is not the primary cause of red colors.
AI.conclusion: The KiDS-selected LSBG candidates are predominantly genuine low surface brightness galaxies, and the sample provides a well-characterized structural reference set for LSBGs in the HSC footprint.

title: Effects of the Background Magnetic Field on Flux Rope Eruptions
summary: Solar eruptive events are generally believed to involve magnetic flux ropes (MFR), formed either in the pre-eruptive phase of the event or during the eruption itself. These MFR eruptions exhibit significant complexity and variations due to the interplay of the physical mechanisms involved, in particular magnetic reconnection and ideal instabilities. This work considers the effect of the background magnetic field on the nature of eruptions with pre-existing MFRs. We used a new MHD model to simulate the whole MFR eruption process, including the pre-eruptive stage and the initiation. Three simulations were performed, all of which used an identical bipolar active region, but with different background magnetic fields in the three cases. The simulations resulted in two successful eruptions (CMEs) and one failed eruption (a confined flare). We analyzed the energetics and the acceleration of the MFR in detail, and found a transition to a rapid exponential rise phase in two of the simulations. We also calculated the criterion for the torus instability and the timing of the breakout and flare reconnections. Our results show that the rapid exponential rise phase is likely due to breakout reconnection. We conclude that a background field antiparallel to the active-region field lowers the magnetic free-energy threshold for eruption; but, does not guarantee a successful eruption. We also found that an antiparallel background field leads to faster flare reconnection, but of shorter duration. Our findings underscore the importance of the background magnetic field in understanding CMEs.

AI.tldr: The paper uses MHD simulations to study how background magnetic fields affect eruptions of pre-existing magnetic flux ropes, showing that antiparallel background fields lower the energy threshold for eruptions and influence reconnection dynamics, but do not guarantee successful CMEs.
AI.motivation: To understand the role of the background magnetic field in determining the success or failure of solar eruptions involving pre-existing magnetic flux ropes, given the complexity and variations observed in such events.
AI.method: A new MHD model was used to simulate the entire MFR eruption process (pre-eruptive stage and initiation) under three different background magnetic field configurations, all sharing an identical bipolar active region.
AI.result: Two simulations produced successful CMEs and one a failed eruption (confined flare). The rapid exponential rise phase was linked to breakout reconnection. An antiparallel background field lowered the magnetic free-energy threshold for eruption but did not guarantee success, and led to faster but shorter-duration flare reconnection.
AI.conclusion: The background magnetic field plays a critical role in solar eruption dynamics: an antiparallel configuration lowers the energy threshold for eruption and alters reconnection characteristics, but success is not assured.

title: The SPHEREx View of Galaxy Clusters: A Simulation-based Validation of the Forced Photometry Pipeline for Extended Sources
summary: We present a simulation-driven assessment of the performance of the SPHEREx pipeline for galaxy cluster science, focusing on photometry, source blending, survey depth, and photometric redshift accuracy. To do that, we compile a sample of eight galaxy clusters spanning a wide redshift range ($z \approx 0.02$-$1.1$) and develop an end-to-end pipeline. We use the ancillary data from the DESI Legacy Survey and COSMOS survey, and generate realistic mock SPHEREx observations with the SPHEREx Sky Simulator. By performing forced photometry on these images with The Tractor, we quantify the characteristic biases and uncertainties relevant to cluster science. We find that the photometry is generally unbiased, but source blending is the primary driver of catastrophic outliers, particularly when the combined flux of neighbors is comparable to the flux of targets. Measuring the effective survey depth, we find that SPHEREx detects members down to $K_{s}\approx 20$ AB ($5σ$), 7-9 mag fainter than the brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) in nearby clusters but only 1-2 mag for clusters at $z \sim 1$, where the BCG itself has faded close to this depth. Despite these challenges, we demonstrate that SPHEREx can achieve a photometric redshift precision of $σ_{\mathrm{NMAD}}\approx 0.003$-$0.01$ for cluster galaxies with an appropriate sample selection based on brightness or signal-to-noise. Combining the redshifts of quality-selected members, we recover cluster redshifts with a bias of $|Δz|/(1+z) < 0.002$ and a scatter of $σ\approx 0.002$ at $z \lesssim 0.5$, meeting the precision required for cluster cosmology.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the SPHEREx survey pipeline for galaxy cluster science using simulations of eight clusters (z≈0.02-1.1). It finds unbiased photometry, blending-driven outliers, survey depths reaching Ks≈20 AB, and photometric redshift precision σ_NMAD≈0.003-0.01 for cluster galaxies, enabling cluster redshift recovery with |Δz|/(1+z)<0.002 bias and σ≈0.002 scatter at z≲0.5.
AI.motivation: To assess the feasibility and performance of the SPHEREx mission for galaxy cluster science, particularly in photometry, blending, depth, and photometric redshift accuracy, before real data are available.
AI.method: Compiled eight galaxy clusters at z≈0.02-1.1; used DESI Legacy Survey and COSMOS ancillary data; generated realistic mock SPHEREx observations using the SPHEREx Sky Simulator; performed forced photometry with The Tractor; quantified biases and uncertainties for cluster science.
AI.result: Photometry is generally unbiased; blending is the main cause of catastrophic outliers; effective depth reaches Ks≈20 AB (5σ); photometric redshift precision σ_NMAD≈0.003-0.01 for cluster galaxies; cluster redshifts recovered with |Δz|/(1+z)<0.002 bias and σ≈0.002 scatter at z≲0.5.
AI.conclusion: SPHEREx can meet the precision required for cluster cosmology with appropriate sample selection, despite blending and depth challenges at high redshift.

title: The Effects of Energy Conservation in Simulating Solar Eruptions
summary: Strict energy conservation is, perhaps, the most basic principle in all physics, but has proven to be difficult to satisfy in numerical simulations of solar eruptions. The Alfvén Wave Solar atmosphere Model (AWSoM) is used to perform a rigorous comparison of CME simulations whose only difference is the use of a conservative vs. non-conservative scheme for the energy equation. A simple, symmetric active region is assumed for the initial magnetic field. As expected, the different numerical schemes result in very different plasma thermal energy, but surprisingly, we also find a factor $>2$ difference in the final kinetic energy, with the energy substantially larger in the energy-conservative scheme. The increase in thermal energy is comparable to the increase in kinetic energy in the conservative simulation. Our analysis reveals that the flare reconnection and increase of kinetic energy terminate earlier with the non-conservative scheme. We conclude that the plasma thermodynamics plays a critical role in the flare reconnection, with the thermal pressure gradient in the current sheet slowing down the reconnection. Our results imply that using strict energy-conservative numerics is critical for space weather modeling of CMEs and for understanding the CME energy budget partitioning.

AI.tldr: This paper compares conservative vs. non-conservative energy schemes in CME simulations using the AWSoM model, finding that energy-conservative numerics produce significantly larger kinetic and thermal energies, with flare reconnection terminating earlier in non-conservative schemes due to thermal pressure gradients in the current sheet.
AI.motivation: Strict energy conservation is a fundamental physics principle but is difficult to satisfy in numerical simulations of solar eruptions, motivating a rigorous comparison of conservative vs. non-conservative schemes for the energy equation in CME modeling.
AI.method: The AWSoM (Alfvén Wave Solar atmosphere Model) is used with a simple, symmetric active region for the initial magnetic field to compare CME simulations that differ only in using a conservative vs. non-conservative scheme for the energy equation.
AI.result: Different numerical schemes yield very different plasma thermal energy; surprisingly, there is a factor >2 difference in final kinetic energy (larger in the conservative scheme). Thermal energy increase is comparable to kinetic energy increase. Flare reconnection and kinetic energy increase terminate earlier with the non-conservative scheme.
AI.conclusion: Plasma thermodynamics critically affects flare reconnection, with the thermal pressure gradient in the current sheet slowing reconnection. Strict energy-conservative numerics are essential for space weather modeling of CMEs and understanding CME energy budget partitioning.

title: A Virgo Environmental Survey Tracing Ionised Gas Emission (VESTIGE) XX. Star formation in the tidal tail of NGC 4254
summary: ALMA 12CO(1-0) observations of 42 star-forming regions located outside the disc of the Virgo Cluster galaxy NGC4254 within an HI gas tail produced during the galaxy's interaction with another cluster member have revealed the presence of ten giant molecular clouds (GMCs) in four of these regions. All of the GMCs were resolved at the angular resolution of the observations (~160 pc) and have molecular gas masses of M(H2)~(0.8-2.0)x10^6} Mo. These ten clouds are characterised by gas column densities [S(H2)~10 Mo pc^-2] and velocity dispersions [sigma_v(CO)~3-12 km s^-1] respectively lower and comparable to those encountered in similar GMCs in the Milky Way. They follow the relation between the gas column density and the star formation activity (Schmidt law) derived using similar data over the stellar disc of NGC4254 and other local and Virgo cluster galaxies. With analytic calculations and tuned simulations, we show that these clouds are unstable and thus expected to dissolve on relatively short timescales (~10-30 Myr). We show that they probably formed after the collapse of dense gas clouds in the HI gas tail stripped during the gravitational interaction that the galaxy suffered several hundreds millions of years ago. The clouds are short-lived and isolated given the low density of the surrounding intracluster medium, which cannot confine the gas expelled by stellar feedback. We discuss the implications of these results in the general context of the fate of stripped gas in hostile cluster environments.

AI.tldr: ALMA 12CO(1-0) observations of 42 star-forming regions in an HI gas tail outside NGC4254's disc reveal ten giant molecular clouds (GMCs) with masses ~(0.8-2.0)x10^6 M☉, lower column densities, and comparable velocity dispersions to Milky Way GMCs. They follow the Schmidt law, are unstable, short-lived (~10-30 Myr), formed from collapsing dense gas in the stripped HI tail, and cannot be confined by the low-density intracluster medium.
AI.motivation: To investigate the properties, formation, and fate of giant molecular clouds in stripped gas tails outside galaxy discs, in the context of galaxy interactions and cluster environments.
AI.method: ALMA 12CO(1-0) observations of 42 star-forming regions in an HI gas tail of NGC4254; resolved GMC analysis via angular resolution (~160 pc); analytic calculations and tuned simulations for cloud stability and timescales.
AI.result: Ten GMCs detected in four regions; masses M(H2)~(0.8-2.0)x10^6 M☉; column densities ~10 M☉ pc^-2 (lower than Milky Way); velocity dispersions σ_v(CO)~3-12 km s^-1 (comparable to Milky Way); follow the Schmidt law; unstable with dissolution timescales ~10-30 Myr.
AI.conclusion: These GMCs are short-lived, isolated, formed from collapsed dense gas in the stripped HI tail, and will dissolve quickly as the low-density intracluster medium cannot confine feedback-driven gas. This informs the fate of stripped gas in hostile cluster environments.

title: The Curious Case of Dark Faculae on M Dwarf Stars
comment: Accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: The study of exoplanet atmospheres has brought a renewed interest in stellar astrophysics. Specifically, stellar magnetic activity from the host star contaminates exoplanet atmosphere transmission spectra, as evidenced by observations from the James Webb Space Telescope. The stellar surface magnetic features in the form of dark spots caused by large concentrations of surface magnetic fields and more diffuse and extended faculae caused by small-scale magnetic field concentrations change the apparent size of the star in a wavelength-dependent way. This spot and faculae contribution to the change in transit depth contaminates the planetary signal. Here we study the transition from bright faculae on G- and K-dwarfs to dark faculae on M-dwarfs. This dark appearance of faculae is in significant contrast to the conventional picture that faculae are brighter than the quiet star region as they are on the Sun. We use the 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamics code MURaM to simulate faculae, and calculate the faculae spectra with the MPS-ATLAS radiative transfer code. We present a qualitative explanation for the transition from dark to bright faculae attributing it to shallower flux tubes and reduced vertical temperature gradients at the surfaces of M dwarfs relative to the Sun.

AI.tldr: This paper uses 3D MHD simulations to study how faculae on M-dwarfs appear dark (unlike the bright faculae on the Sun and G/K-dwarfs), which affects exoplanet transmission spectroscopy by changing stellar apparent size in a wavelength-dependent manner.
AI.motivation: Stellar magnetic activity contaminates exoplanet atmosphere transmission spectra (as seen by JWST). Understanding how spots and faculae change the apparent size of the star is crucial for disentangling planetary signals from stellar contamination, especially the poorly understood behavior of faculae on cooler M-dwarfs.
AI.method: Used the 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamics code MURaM to simulate faculae on M-dwarfs, and calculated faculae spectra with the MPS-ATLAS radiative transfer code.
AI.result: Faculae on M-dwarfs appear dark, in contrast to the conventional picture where faculae are brighter than the quiet star region (as on the Sun and G/K-dwarfs). This transition from bright to dark faculae is explained by shallower flux tubes and reduced vertical temperature gradients at the surfaces of M-dwarfs.
AI.conclusion: The dark appearance of faculae on M-dwarfs significantly alters the wavelength-dependent stellar contamination in exoplanet transmission spectra, requiring revised models for interpreting JWST observations of exoplanet atmospheres around low-mass stars.

title: A Consistent Comparison of Intracluster Light Assembly in Simulations I. Redshift Evolution and Progenitor Galaxies
comment: 25 pages, 14 figures, accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
summary: The tidal stripping of satellite galaxies and the stellar detritus ejected during galaxy mergers builds up a diffuse stellar component in galaxy clusters known as the intracluster light (ICL). We investigate ICL assembly in cluster-mass haloes ($M_{178c}\sim10^{14}-10^{15}$ M$_\odot$) using four different hydrodynamical simulations (Horizon-AGN, TNG100, The Three Hundred Gizmo-Simba 7K, and Hydrangea) under a homogenized ICL identification framework. For our fiducial ICL definition we obtain broadly consistent $z\approx0$ ICL stellar mass fractions ($\sim0.1-0.2$) and, by tracking the progenitors of $z\approx0$ clusters back to $z\gtrsim2$, find no significant evolution in average ICL mass fractions. Alternative approaches for distinguishing the ICL from the central galaxy show the absolute ICL fraction to be highly sensitive to adopted definition, but we never find any significant inter-simulation discrepancies when implementing a consistent methodology to identify the ICL. Whether the average ICL mass fraction falls with increasing redshift or does not evolve is determined by the ICL definition adopted. By tracing $z\approx0$ ICL stars back to their progenitor galaxies, we find that lower-mass satellites typically make slightly larger ICL contributions relative to their mass in every considered simulation, but which galaxies make the dominant contribution to the ICL is primarily controlled by the infalling satellite mass function. Most ICL stars sourced from satellite galaxies are therefore expected to originate from galaxies with infall stellar masses above $\sim10^{10}$ M$_\odot$ and largely within $10^{10.5}-10^{11.5}$ M$_\odot$.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the assembly of intracluster light (ICL) in cluster-mass haloes using four different hydrodynamical simulations under a homogenized ICL identification framework. It finds broadly consistent ICL stellar mass fractions (~0.1-0.2) at z≈0, no significant evolution in average ICL mass fractions, and that lower-mass satellites contribute more ICL relative to their mass, but dominant ICL contributions come from galaxies with infall stellar masses of ~10^10.5-10^11.5 M⊙.
AI.motivation: To understand how intracluster light (ICL) assembles in galaxy clusters and to reconcile apparent discrepancies between different hydrodynamical simulations regarding ICL properties by applying a homogenized ICL identification framework.
AI.method: Four hydrodynamical simulations (Horizon-AGN, TNG100, The Three Hundred Gizmo-Simba 7K, Hydrangea) were analyzed using a consistent ICL identification framework. Progenitor tracking from z≈0 back to z≳2 was performed, and ICL stars were traced to their progenitor galaxies to determine contributions.
AI.result: At z≈0, ICL stellar mass fractions are broadly consistent (~0.1-0.2) across simulations. No significant evolution in average ICL mass fractions was found. Lower-mass satellites contribute more ICL relative to their mass, but the dominant ICL contribution comes from galaxies with infall stellar masses of 10^10.5-10^11.5 M⊙. The absolute ICL fraction is highly sensitive to definition, but consistent methodology eliminates inter-simulation discrepancies.
AI.conclusion: ICL assembly is robustly consistent across different simulations when a homogenized framework is applied. The ICL fraction's redshift evolution is definition-dependent. The infalling satellite mass function primarily controls which galaxies dominate ICL production, with most ICL stars originating from intermediate-mass galaxies (10^10.5-10^11.5 M⊙).

title: Once more: Leaky MHD waves in coronal magnetic flux tubes
summary: By a detailed comparison of leaky magnetohydrodynamic waves in coronal magnetic flux tubes with leaky electromagnetic waves in dielectric media it is shown that the latter kind may be called quasi-normal modes, since they can be regularised by a normalisation which systematically cuts off the contribution of the external homogeneous region, whereas such a possibility is forbidden for the former kind by the conservation of magnetic flux. Consequently, leaky magnetohydrodynamic waves cannot be systematically applied to coronal seismology, i.e. to the inverse spectral problem of determining the different equilibrium distributions of the fields by comparing the spectra they produce with the observed ones.

AI.tldr: Leaky MHD waves in coronal flux tubes cannot be regularized like leaky EM waves in dielectrics due to magnetic flux conservation, making them unsuitable for coronal seismology.
AI.motivation: To examine whether leaky magnetohydrodynamic waves in coronal magnetic flux tubes can be systematically applied to coronal seismology, by comparing them with leaky electromagnetic waves in dielectric media.
AI.method: Detailed comparison of leaky MHD waves in coronal magnetic flux tubes with leaky EM waves in dielectric media, analyzing regularization possibilities and the role of magnetic flux conservation.
AI.result: Leaky EM waves in dielectrics can be regularized as quasi-normal modes via a normalization that cuts off the external homogeneous region contribution, but leaky MHD waves cannot be similarly regularized due to magnetic flux conservation.
AI.conclusion: Leaky MHD waves cannot be systematically applied to coronal seismology (inverse spectral problem of determining equilibrium field distributions from observed spectra).

title: Abundances of CNO in candidate young metal-poor stars
summary: In this contribution we investigate the CNO abundances in five apparently young evolved stars, with the aim of discriminating between truly young stars and stars that were rejuvenated by accreting mass from another star. Stars that have accreted mass are expected to show low C and O and a very low [C/O] ratio, as displayed by some stars in the Globular Cluster 47 Tuc, that are believed to have undergone mass-transfer. In our sample the low [C/O] ratios observed appear to be compatible with their evolutionary status. There is thus no indication for these stars having accreted mass.__

AI.tldr: This paper investigates CNO abundances in five young evolved stars to distinguish truly young stars from those rejuvenated by mass accretion. The low [C/O] ratios observed in the sample are consistent with their evolutionary status, showing no evidence of mass transfer.
AI.motivation: To discriminate between truly young evolved stars and stars that appear young due to rejuvenation via mass accretion from a companion, using CNO abundance patterns as diagnostic tools.
AI.method: Measurement and analysis of CNO abundances in five apparently young evolved stars, comparing their [C/O] ratios to known signatures of mass transfer (low C, O, and very low [C/O]) as seen in 47 Tuc stars.
AI.result: The low [C/O] ratios observed in the sample are compatible with the stars' evolutionary status, and no indications of mass accretion were found.
AI.conclusion: The five apparently young evolved stars show no evidence of having accreted mass; their CNO abundances are consistent with genuine youth rather than rejuvenation via mass transfer.

title: Solar Wind Dependence on Source Distance from the Open-Closed Boundary
summary: The origin and variability of the slow solar wind remains an open question in solar physics, but is thought to be closely linked to dynamics at the Sun's open-closed magnetic flux boundary (OCB). Interchange magnetic reconnection at the OCB has been proposed as a mechanism for releasing closed-field plasma into the heliosphere, but observational evidence linking solar wind composition to OCB topology remains limited. We relate in situ solar wind measurements by Ulysses over a 10-year period to the magnetic topology of their source regions using two coronal magnetic field models: a potential field source surface model and a magnetofrictional model. We find a strong dependence of solar wind composition on the distance of the source magnetic flux from the OCB. Enhanced ion charge-state ratios, elemental abundances, and compositional variability are found to be concentrated within a supergranular-scale region (around 25 Mm) surrounding the OCB, consistent with the spatial scales of interchange magnetic reconnection. This variability decreases systematically with increasing distance from the boundary, with coronal hole wind exhibiting more uniform fast-wind signatures. We also find that the composition of solar wind emerging from regions close to the OCB is influenced by the strength of neighbouring closed magnetic fields, with stronger fields preferentially associated with slow-wind properties. These results indicate that the composition of the slow wind is strongly governed by the magnetic topology of the OCB, providing compelling evidence that interchange reconnection plays a crucial role in slow solar wind release and structure.

AI.tldr: The slow solar wind's composition and variability are strongly linked to magnetic topology near the open-closed flux boundary (OCB), with supergranular-scale (≈25 Mm) enhancement of compositional signatures consistent with interchange reconnection, providing direct evidence that interchange reconnection governs slow solar wind release.
AI.motivation: The origin and variability of the slow solar wind remain an open question in solar physics, and is thought to be linked to dynamics at the Sun's open-closed magnetic flux boundary (OCB). Observational evidence linking solar wind composition to OCB topology has been limited.
AI.method: The authors relate in situ solar wind measurements from Ulysses (10-year period) to magnetic topology of source regions using two coronal magnetic field models: a potential field source surface (PFSS) model and a magnetofrictional (MF) model.
AI.result: (1) Strong dependence of solar wind composition on source flux distance from OCB; (2) enhanced ion charge-state ratios, elemental abundances, and compositional variability concentrated in a ~25 Mm supergranular-scale region around the OCB; (3) variability decreases systematically with distance from OCB; (4) composition near OCB is influenced by the strength of neighboring closed magnetic fields, with stronger fields associated with slow-wind properties.
AI.conclusion: Solar wind composition is strongly governed by the magnetic topology of the OCB, providing compelling evidence that interchange reconnection plays a crucial role in slow solar wind release and structure.

title: UCLCHEM 4.0: An open source gas-grain astrochemistry simulation framework
comment: Submitted to RAS Techniques and Instruments
summary: Astrochemical modeling is a key tool for the understanding of the formation and destruction of molecules in the dense gas of the interstellar medium, as observed by modern day observational facilities. UCLCHEM is a comprehensive astrochemical modeling framework that can model the interstellar medium ranging from extra-galactic to protoplanetary disks scales. The framework consists of a core routine that solves chemical reaction networks as a function of time. The chemistry includes a description of gas and ice grain chemistry and the interactions between the two. The physical modeling includes parametrizations for modelling cloud collapse, protostellar cores and shocks as well as the ability to provide user defined inputs. This manuscript provides an overview of the physics and chemistry included in UCLCHEM, as well as the inner workings of the solver routine and the programming interface.

AI.tldr: UCLCHEM is a comprehensive astrochemical modeling framework for simulating molecular formation and destruction in interstellar medium, spanning from extra-galactic to protoplanetary disk scales, with gas/ice grain chemistry, physical parametrizations for various astrophysical environments, and a solver routine for chemical reaction networks.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive astrochemical modeling framework that bridges the gap between observational facilities and theoretical understanding of molecular formation and destruction in the dense gas of the interstellar medium across multiple scales.
AI.method: The framework solves chemical reaction networks as a function of time using a core routine, incorporates gas and ice grain chemistry with grain-surface interactions, and includes physical parametrizations for cloud collapse, protostellar cores, shocks, and user-defined inputs.
AI.result: A versatile astrochemical modeling framework (UCLCHEM) capable of modeling environments from extra-galactic to protoplanetary disk scales, with detailed gas-grain chemistry and multiple physical parametrization options.
AI.conclusion: UCLCHEM provides an overview of its physics, chemistry, solver routine inner workings, and programming interface for astrochemical modeling applications.

title: Intermittent turbulent fluctuations in solar coronal mass ejections
summary: Localised regions of high intensity fluctuations are known to be signatures of intermittency in fluid and plasma turbulence. We investigate such turbulent spots using near-Earth {\em in-situ} spacecraft observations of a sample of 125 solar coronal mass ejections (CMEs). We present statistical results which suggest that the intensity of the strongest turbulent spot and the turbulent spot occurrence rate are reliable indicators of the onset of the leading part of the CME event. Our findings also suggest that turbulent spots can be sites of enhanced proton heating. The findings of this study can enhance our understanding of intermittence in collisionless plasma turbulence and can improve CME/sheath-driven space weather impact prediction models.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes turbulent spots (intermittency signatures) in 125 solar coronal mass ejections using spacecraft data, finding that turbulent spot intensity and occurrence rate reliably indicate CME onset, and that these spots are sites of enhanced proton heating, with implications for space weather prediction.
AI.motivation: To investigate localized high-intensity fluctuations (turbulent spots) as signatures of intermittency in collisionless plasma turbulence, specifically within coronal mass ejections, and to assess their utility as indicators of CME onset and proton heating.
AI.method: Statistical analysis of in-situ spacecraft observations of 125 solar coronal mass ejections, examining turbulent spot characteristics (intensity, occurrence rate) relative to CME event onset and proton heating signatures.
AI.result: The strongest turbulent spot intensity and turbulent spot occurrence rate are reliable indicators of the leading part of CME onset. Turbulent spots are identified as sites of enhanced proton heating.
AI.conclusion: The findings enhance understanding of intermittency in collisionless plasma turbulence and can improve CME/sheath-driven space weather impact prediction models.

title: A merger shock traced by radio arcs and ultra-long radio tails in galaxy cluster A2142
summary: Abell 2142 (A2142) is a massive, nearby galaxy cluster undergoing a complex merger. It exhibits an elongated X-ray morphology along the northwest-southeast axis and hosts four known cold fronts. Using XMM-Newton observations, we detect a merger shock on the northwest side of the cluster with a Mach number of $M \sim 1.3$. The observed shock front and four cold fronts can be reproduced by numerical simulations of an off-axis merger with a large impact parameter, which imparts significant angular momentum to induce the sloshing of the subcluster core and large-scale ambient gas. In projection, the shock front is spatially coincident with arc-shaped radio filaments observed behind the prominent head-tail radio galaxies T1 and T2. We interpret these radio arcs as partial vortex ring structures (resembling ``smoke rings'') produced by the interaction of the merger shock with the low-density cocoons of radio galaxies. The shock strips and rolls the jet cocoon into a toroidal vortex, as predicted by recent magnetohydrodynamic simulations. We further demonstrate that the merger shock can significantly elongate the radio tails by re-accelerating aged relativistic electrons and stretching the tail plasma via the post-shock wind. This process provides a natural explanation for the $>$500 kpc tail observed in this and other merging clusters. Our findings establish radio arcs and ultra-long radio tails as independent, complementary tracers of merger shocks in galaxy clusters. Our results demonstrate that merger shocks can reshape both the thermal and non-thermal components of galaxy clusters, and that tailed radio galaxies serve as sensitive probes of intracluster medium weather.

AI.tldr: XMM-Newton observations of A2142 detect a Mach ~1.3 merger shock coincident with radio arcs (vortex rings from shock-cocoon interaction) and ultra-long radio tails (>500 kpc) from re-acceleration and post-shock stretching; merger shocks reshape both thermal and non-thermal ICM components.
AI.motivation: To understand how merger shocks in galaxy clusters interact with both thermal (X-ray) and non-thermal (radio) components, and to establish radio arcs and ultra-long radio tails as complementary tracers of merger shocks in complex merging systems like A2142.
AI.method: XMM-Newton X-ray observations to detect merger shock and cold fronts; numerical simulations of off-axis merger with large impact parameter to reproduce observed morphology; comparison with radio observations to identify shock-induced radio arcs and elongated tails.
AI.result: Detected a merger shock with Mach ~1.3 on the northwest side; reproduced four cold fronts and shock front via off-axis merger simulations; shock front spatially coincides with arc-shaped radio filaments (vortex rings); merger shock can produce radio tails >500 kpc via re-acceleration and post-shock stretching.
AI.conclusion: Radio arcs and ultra-long radio tails serve as independent, complementary tracers of merger shocks; merger shocks reshape both thermal and non-thermal ICM; tailed radio galaxies are sensitive probes of ICM weather.

title: V7995 Sgr: A New FU Orionis Accretion Outburst Near NGC 6589/6590
summary: We announce a new FU Orionis type outburst that reached peak brightness in late 2024, following a steep 4.6 month photometric rise of -2.85 mag in the $r$ band. This rapid brightening at all wavelengths was preceeded in the infrared by a much shallower rise over 4 years. The progenitor object was an unstudied young stellar object having a flat-spectrum type spectral energy distribution, and extended nebulosity. We present multi-wavelength lightcurves covering the photometric low-state, the outburst, and early post-outburst epochs. Optical imaging shows a concurrent brightening of the extended nebular environment. We also present follow-up optical/near-infrared spectroscopy taken 1.5 years after the inferred photometric peak. The spectra confirm an FU Ori type outburst. The outburst source exhibits a mixed-temperature absorption spectrum, formed in an accretion disk, and it shows several line species with blueshifted absorption profiles that are formed in a strong wind.

AI.tldr: A new FU Orionis-type outburst was detected in late 2024, showing a rapid 2.85 mag brightening in r-band over 4.6 months, preceded by a shallow 4-year infrared rise. The progenitor is a flat-spectrum YSO with nebulosity. Multi-wavelength lightcurves and optical/near-IR spectroscopy confirm a mixed-temperature accretion disk spectrum with blueshifted absorption features from a strong wind.
AI.motivation: To report and characterize a newly identified FU Orionis-type outburst event that reached peak brightness in late 2024, providing observational data from pre-outburst through post-outburst phases.
AI.method: Multi-wavelength photometric monitoring covering pre-outburst, outburst, and post-outburst epochs; optical imaging of the nebular environment; and follow-up optical/near-infrared spectroscopy taken 1.5 years after peak brightness.
